name: Combat
content:
When combat or some other tense situation arises and it becomes necessary to track the action carefully, special rules apply governing characters' actions.

It is the GM's responsibility to decide when the game should move into and out of combat.

ENTERING COMBAT

To enter combat, follow these steps:

1) GROUP COMBATANTS

Start by dividing all combatants into GROUPS. A group is a unit of allied combatants who act together as combat progresses. Often there will be just two groups: player characters and foes. In more complex situations, the GM may choose to create additional groups: allies, additional foes, non-combatants, or even environmental factors like a collapsing bridge, an erupting volcano, etc.

If players characters are separated by a significant distance or are otherwise divided in a way that would prevent them from coordinating their efforts, the GM may choose to create multiple groups of player characters.

Once groups are established, it's time to establish Initiative:

2) ROLL INITIATIVE

To determine the INITIATIVE order among the groups, each member of each group rolls one feat die (d12) and adds their WITS score to the result. Add together the highest result and lowest result among the group to determine that group’s total initiative result.

If a group only includes a single combatant, its single Initiative roll is the total for its group.

Compare all groups' total Initiative results to determine the Initiative order for the combat. If there is a tie, each tied group rolls a single feat die as a tiebreaker.

Initiative Rolls that produce Sol 🌞 or Morte 💀 contribute to BANE/BOON for the Quest, and Morte 💀 triggers a Soft Move from GM, as with Skill Checks.

Any combatant that rolls Morte 💀 on their Initiative roll is caught off guard and may not during the first regular round of combat, nor can they act during the Surprise Round:

3) SURPRISE ROUND

Before combat begins in earnest, there may be a SURPRISE ROUND.

Any combatant that rolls Sol 🌞 on their Initiative Roll gets to act during the Surprise Round. Only the combatant that rolled Sol 🌞 - not their whole group - gets to act in the Surprise Round. Any number of combatants from any number of groups may act in the Surprise Round.

In the Surprise Round, combatants take turns individually rather than in groups. Compare individual Initiative rolls to determine the order of turns for the Surprise Round.

If a group wants to attempt an ambush, each member of the ambushing group rolls Stealth and each member of the target group rolls Awareness. For each group, add together the highest and lowest result to get that group's total. If the ambushing group's total is higher, each member of that group automatically gets to act in the Surprise Round, regardless of their Initiative Roll for the combat. Otherwise, roll Initiative as normal.

ROUNDS OF COMBAT

Combat progresses in ROUNDS. Each Round represents 5 seconds of in-game time, and each group gets the Initiative once per Round.

When a group has the Initiative, each member of the group takes a turn - in whatever order they choose among themselves - before moving on to the next group. The order of turns among members of a group may vary from round to round.

TAKING A TURN

Each combatant has the following options available to them on each of their turns:

  • MOVEMENT: You may move a distance up to your Speed. You can break up your movement, moving before, after or in between actions. Any combination is fine as long as your total movement for the turn is within your speed.

  • TAKE ACTIONS: By default, combatants have 1 ½ actions available to them per Round. Many Abilities cost one Action or one Half Action to activate. There are also some standard Combat Actions that are always available to all combatants (see Combat Actions below). You may use any combination of Actions and/or Half Actions each turn: one Action and one Half Action, three Half Actions, etc.

  • REACTIONS: By default, combatants have 1 Reaction available to them per Round. Reactions are special Abilities that have a specified Trigger condition and may be activated at any time during the round (not just on your turn).

  • FREE ACTIONS: Combatants may take any number of Free Actions on their turn. Some Abilities are Free Actions, but Free Actions also encompass such activities as brief communication, gestures, or simple interactions with objects, like opening or closing a door, pulling a lever, picking up or dropping an item, sheathing or pulling out a weapon, etc. The GM can rule what can be reasonably considered a Free Action.

COMBAT ACTIONS

In addition to your character's Abilities, the following options are always available to you in combat. Each costs 1 Action:

ATTACK - You make a single melee or ranged Attack. Describe your attack.

SPRINT - You move up to your Speed. This is in addition to your normal Movement for the turn. Describe your sprint.

HELP - You grant a +1d bonus to another creature's next Skill Check for a specific task this round. The GM determines whether the task is something you can reasonably help with. Describe how you help.

EVADE - Choose one: 1) You avoid Opportunity Attacks this turn. 2) Until your next turn, attacks against you from combatants you can see are Ill-Favored and your Dexterity checks are favored. Either way, describe how you evade.

SKILL CHECKS IN COMBAT

When attempting an action outside of your explicit Abilities during your turn, the GM may call for a Skill Check. The GM is responsible for determining what can be reasonably accomplished through a Skill Check on a combat turn, whether it costs an Action or Half Action to attempt, what is an appropriate Difficulty and what effects it might produce.

Examples: Use Stealth to hide; Use Awe to intimidate foes; Use Craft to improvise a barricade.

SPECIAL MOVEMENT

Climbing, crawling, swimming, navigating difficult terrain and any other inhibited movement all costs twice as much movement to accomplish. For example, swimming through 10 feet of water requires 20 feet of movement.

In general, you're able to move through space occupied by allies, but not through space occupied by foes or other obstacles. The GM has discretion to determine where you can and cannot move.

Combatants that are able to fly are able to move through the air up to their Speed, but if they are knocked prone, their speed is reduced to 0, or they are otherwise made unable to move, they fall to the ground.

PRONE

While prone, you automatically lose Engagements, your attack rolls are Ill-Favored and Ranged attacks against you from further away than short range are Ill-Favored. To stand up from prone, you must spend half your movement on your turn. Otherwise, your only movement option is to crawl. You may fall prone on your turn as a Free Action.

FALLING

Falling to the ground from a height deals 1d6 damage for every 10 feet fallen. Additionally, for every 20 feet fallen, roll Injury (see Injury below). For example, a creature that falls from a height of 40 feet would take 4d6 damage and roll Injury twice.

By default, a creature lands prone at the end of a fall. The GM may allow for a Skill Check (commonly Dexterity) to attempt to land on your feet.

JUMPING, LIFTING, PUSHING, PULLING

You can jump a distance equal to your height from a standing position, or twice that distance with a running start of at least 10 feet. Either way, the maximum height of your jump is half your height, and the jump distance counts as movement.

You can lift, push or pull objects weighing up to your own weight.

The GM may allow you to attempt to exceed these limits with a Skill Check.

REACH & OPPORTUNITY ATTACKS

REACH is the distance at which a combatant can make melee attacks without moving from their current position. By default, combatants control a 5 foot square in combat and their Reach extends to each of the 5 foot squares adjacent to their own. Larger or smaller combatants may take up more or less space and have longer or shorter Reach.

Abilities and Equipment that augment Reach or provide their own Reach extend a combatant's existing Reach. For example, a combatant with standard Reach who is wielding a polearm with Reach: 5 is able to attack foes out to 10 feet - foes who are TWO 5 ft squares out from their own.

Whenever one combatant leaves another's Reach, the latter may use a Reaction to make a single melee attack against them, immediately, skipping Engagement (see Attacks & Damage below).

DRAG, SHOVE & GRAPPLE

Attempting to drag, shove or grapple with a combatant is resolved via an Opposed Skill Check - most often, Strength vs Strength.

Melee and Ranged attacks against a grappled creature are Favored. To attempt to escape a grapple, the creature may spend an Action to repeat the Opposed Skill Check. On a win, they escape. On a loss, they remain grappled.

COVER

If an obstacle completely blocks all lines of attack between an attacker and target for a Melee or Ranged Attack, or for a Spell that requires sight, the Attack or Spell cannot proceed. If half or more of the target is obscured, the attack is Ill-Favored. If less than half of the target is obscured, the Attack proceeds as normal.

The GM may require a Skill Check to gain Cover in questionable circumstances.

SWITCHING WEAPONS

You may put away OR pull out a weapon as a Free Action, as mentioned. To put away one weapon AND pull out another weapon, the cost is a Half Action. Alternately, you may drop a weapon as a Free Action, then pull out another weapon as a Free Action. The GM may rule what can be reasonably done with Free Actions in a turn.

DELAYING

You may delay your entire turn or a portion of it. To do so, declare a specific trigger that will prompt your delayed turn (or part of it) and state exactly what you intend to do (e.g., “I will run to the door if the ogre moves away from it.”). You may delay movement, part of your movement, or one or more Actions, Half Actions, or Free Actions.

When the declared trigger occurs, you immediately resolve the delayed turn or part of your turn. If the trigger does not occur before the end of the Round, resolve the delay as follows:

  • If you delayed your entire turn, you take it at the end of the Round.

  • If you delayed only part of your turn, that part is forfeited.

After resolving your delayed turn (or portion of it), you rejoin your group in the Initiative order in the next Round.

ATTACKS & DAMAGE

Any ability that inflicts harm or imposes the will of another on one or more unwilling creatures is considered an ATTACK. Attacks can employ many different mechanics, but most follow two common patterns:

  • The attacker rolls a Skill Check against a Difficulty equal to one of the target’s stats (Defense is the default for physical attacks).

  • The attacker and target each make an Opposed Skill Check against each other.

The Skill Check or the attacker's side of the Opposed Skill Check are referred to as the Attack Roll for the Attack.

Attacks have a wide range of effects when successful, but many Attacks call for a Damage Roll:

DAMAGE ROLLS

The number and type(s) of dice rolled for a DAMAGE ROLL, as well as any modifiers applied, are determined by the Ability and/or Equipment used. The result of a Damage Roll is always subtracted from the target’s current Endurance.

Renaissance does not use explicit damage types. However, if the nature of the damage is relevant to the situation, the GM may apply bonuses or penalties at their discretion—typically by adding or removing dice from the damage pool, or by doubling or halving the total damage (see Dice Rolls).

MARTIAL TRAINING

Each character has MARTIAL TRAINING for various types of Weapons and Armor. If you make an Attack with a Weapon you are trained for, the Attack Roll is flat by default. If you make an Attack with a Weapon that you are not trained for, the Attack Roll is Ill-Favored by default. See Equipment and Character Creation.

ATTACK TYPES

Various effects interact with, or are triggered by, specific ATTACK TYPES.

All physical attacks are classified as either Melee Attacks or Ranged Attacks. A Melee Attack that benefits from augmented Reach is still considered a Melee Attack. Any attack made with a Weapon is Considered a Weapon Attack.

Melee and Ranged Attacks follow these default mechanics:

  • Melee Attacks are made by rolling Strength against the target’s Defense.

  • Ranged Attacks are made by rolling Dexterity against the target’s Defense.

  • Unarmed Attacks or Attacks using an improvised weapon use a single d4 for Damage Rolls, unless otherwise determined by the GM.

In all of the above cases, add your BODY score to the Damage Roll.

Some magical attacks are defined as Melee Spell Attacks or Ranged Spell Attacks, while others are simply Spell Attacks and are considered neither Melee nor Ranged.

All these types may be combined in various combinations - Ranged Weapon Attack, Melee Spell Attack, etc. - which may interact with various effects, resistances and vulnerabilities.

RANGE & RANGED ATTACKS

Many abilities and equipment items have a Range, which is expressed in five tiers:

ADJACENT = up to 5 feet
SHORT RANGE = up to 25 feet
MEDIUM RANGE = up to 50 feet
LONG RANGE = up to 100 feet
FAR RANGE = up to 200 feet

Ranged attacks against Adjacent creatures are Ill-Favored if the creature can see you.

You may sacrifice accuracy for increased Range. For Ranged Attacks that have a range of Short Range or higher, if the Attack Roll is not already Ill-Favored, you may make it Ill-Favored to double its range.

ENGAGEMENT

Melee combat is rarely a simple case of taking a swing with a weapon. More often, there is an exchange of careful maneuvers and footwork before an attacker attempts to land a blow. This exchange is represented by ENGAGEMENT.

Any time a combatant makes a Melee Attack, they and the target of the Attack enter Engagement, rolling Engagement Dice to determine the outcome of the exchange.

Each combatant has a limited number of Engagement Dice available to them each Round. These dice are generally granted by their martial training and by Equipment they're wearing or wielding. As such, combatants specializing in melee combat are likely to have far more Engagement Dice than those who specialize in other areas.

ENTERING ENGAGEMENT

Each combatant chooses how many of their Engagement Dice they will roll for each Engagement. Since Engagement Dice are a per-Round resource, in some situations it may be advantageous to reserve some dice for other Engagements during the same Round.

The number and types of the dice you’re committing to the Engagement do not have to be declared before rolling. In fact, any and all methods of concealing your dice - or even deceptive tactics like shaking dice in your hand but not actually rolling them - are fair game.

Once both sides have chosen their dice, count down from three and then roll all Engagement Dice simultaneously.

RESOLVING ENGAGEMENT

Compare the highest die result from each side. The side with the higher result in that pair wins the pair. Then compare the next-highest pair, then the next-highest, and so on until all dice have been considered. The side with the most wins wins the Engagement. If there is an equal number of wins on both sides, the Engagement results in a draw.

If one combatant rolls more dice than the other, the unopposed dice count as wins. If one side decides not to roll any Engagement dice, they automatically lose the Engagement. If neither side rolled any dice, it's a draw.

As you resolve each pair of Engagement dice, describe the action and - at the end - how it positions the attacker to strike a blow.

AFTER ENGAGEMENT

Once the Engagement is resolved, the attacker makes their Attack Roll:

  • If the attacker won the Engagement, the Attack Roll is Favored.

  • If the defender won the Engagement, the Attack Roll is Ill-Favored.

  • If the Engagement resulted in a draw, the Attack Roll is unmodified (if it was already Favored or Ill-Favored, it remains so).

SPENDING & REGAINING ENGAGEMENT DICE

As soon as a die is rolled for Engagement, it is considered spent and cannot be used again until it is regained. At the beginning of each combatant's turn, all their spent Engagement Dice are regained.

The 9 and 7 are the highest for each combatant, so we compare them and the attacker wins that pair. The 5 and 3 are the next-highest, so we compare them and, once again, the attacker wins. The remaining d6 from the attacker is unopposed, so that's another win. That's a 3-0 Engagement victory for the attacker, so their Attack Roll is Favored. Both combatants cannot use the dice they rolled in another Engagement until the dice are refreshed at the beginning of their next respective turns.

ENGAGEMENT SUCCESSES

Any time you roll the maximum result on an Engagement die, it is an ENGAGEMENT SUCCESS, which you can spend to achieve various effects during the current Engagement.

The effects available to you are determined by your martial training and by the Equipment you're currently wielding or wearing. Each Ability or Equipment item indicates which Engagement Success effects it contributes. Below are all available Engagement Success effects:

  • BIND - You and your opponent's weapons lock together. The Engagement ends in a draw, immediately (the attack still proceeds).

  • COMPASS - You move around your opponent to any position adjacent to them.

  • DISARM - Your opponent drops a wielded item of your choosing. You may only use this if you have already used another success in this Engagement.

  • FEINT  - You may reroll one of your Engagement Dice.

  • HOOK - Choose one piece of your opponent's Armor or their Shield. They lose the benefits of that item until their next turn.

  • INVITATION - Your opponent must reroll an Engagement Die of your choice.

  • KNOCKBACK - You push your opponent 5 feet back. If this puts either of you outside the other's Reach, the attacker in this Engagement may use additional movement to move within Reach. Otherwise, the Engagement ends immediately and no attack is made. If this is the second time you've used Knockback in this Engagement, the opponent is also knocked prone.

  • MANCHETTE - You land a glancing blow. Your opponent takes 1 Injury.

  • PARRY - You deflect your opponent's incoming maneuver. You win this pair, regardless of who has the higher die result. If your opponent also uses Parry for this pair, the higher die result wins as normal.

  • RETREAT - You move 5 feet away from your opponent. If this puts either of you outside the other's Reach, the attacker in this Engagement may use additional movement to move within Reach. Otherwise, the Engagement ends immediately and no attack is made.

  • RIPOSTE - Make a melee attack against your opponent immediately, skipping Engagement, then return to this Engagement. You may only use this if you have already used another Engagement Success in this Engagement.

  • STUN - All of your opponent's unspent Engagement Dice become spent.

  • SUNDER - Choose one piece of your opponent's Armor or their Shield. That item's Defense bonus, if any, is permanently reduced by 1. If they have no Armor or Shield, or only natural armor, their current Defense is reduced by 1.

Resolve Engagement Successes as you evaluate the pairs they are in. When you evaluate a pair that includes an Engagement Success, the player who rolled the Success declares the effect they will use and resolves that effect before resolving the pair. If both players rolled a Success in a pair, resolve the higher Success result first (there is a tie, flip a coin or roll other dice to break the tie).

If an effect forces a re-roll of either die in a pair that was already resolved, re-resolve that pair, including any new Engagement Successes rolled. If a die that rolled an Engagement Success is forced to re-roll before it is resolved, the original Engagement Success is lost.

You don't have to match specific Engagement Dice with their specific Engagement Success effects. The available effects are pooled together and can be bought with Successes from any of your Engagement Dice.

For example, let's say you're wielding a shield that grants you a d4 Engagement Die and the Parry effect, as well as a war hammer that grants you a d6 Engagement Die and the Knockback effect. If you were to roll a 4 on the d4 or a 6 on the d6, you could spend that success on either Parry OR Knockback.

INJURY

While Endurance is easily lost and easily gained, INJURY represents more severe harm that is more difficult to inflict and more difficult to heal. Injury makes you more vulnerable to the Helpless State, which in turn makes it harder to regain Endurance by resting (see Rest & Recovery).

INFLICTING INJURY

While some Abilities provide special ways to directly inflict Injury on a target, it is possible to inflict Injury with any Attack that requires a Skill Check. If the result of the Skill Check for the attack includes Sol 🌞, the attacker inflicts Injury on the target, even if the overall result of the roll is a failure or loss.

Whenever Injury is inflicted, the target rolls a feat die:

  • On a 1-10, the result is added to the target’s current Injury score.

  • On Sol 🌞, the wound is insignificant - no Injury is inflicted.

  • On Morte 💀, the wound is dire - the target’s Injury score increases to equal their maximum Defense.

For player characters, Injury Rolls that produce Sol 🌞 or Morte 💀 contribute to BANE/BOON for the Quest, and Morte 💀 triggers a Soft Move from GM, as with Skill Checks.

RESISTING INJURY

If an attack inflicts Injury on a creature and the creature is not Helpless, before rolling for Injury, a it may choose to resist the Injury by checking a Condition: they heighten their emotions to avoid the worst of a blow. If they do so, they may roll two feat dice instead of one for their Injury roll and keep the more favorable result. They may only do this only once per Injury roll.

DEATH

KNOCKOUTS & DYING

When your Endurance is reduced to 0, you are knocked unconscious. You fall prone and drop any items you’re carrying that aren’t attached to your body.

While unconscious, your Defense is reduced by your base Defense (10 + WITS), to a minimum of 0. Armor and any other effects augmenting your Defense remain in place.

If you are not Twice Helpless, you wake up after an hour with 1 Endurance. If you are Twice Helpless and unconscious, you are dying: if you don’t return to at least 1 Endurance within an hour, you die.

Anyone may attempt to stabilize a creature that is dying by making an Aid check. The Difficulty is equal to the dying creature's current Injury score + 10. On a pass, they remain at 0 Endurance but are no longer dying. They must regain at least 1 Endurance to wake up.

Any time you wake up from being knocked unconscious, check a Condition.

It is possible to die instantly. When damage reduces you to 0 Endurance and there is damage remaining, you die instantly if the remaining damage equals or exceeds your Endurance maximum.

If an attacker wants to knock a creature unconscious without risk of killing them, they must declare this intent before making their Attack Roll. If they reduce the foe to 0 Endurance, the foe falls unconscious, is stable, and will wake up in one hour with 1 Endurance.

SUFFOCATION & DROWNING

A character can hold their breath for a number of seconds equal to twice their maximum Endurance, rounded up to the nearest 5 seconds. Once that limit is reached, they lose half their current Endurance, rounded up, each turn. If they reach 0 Endurance, follow the normal rules for knockouts and dying.

SPECIAL STATUSES

GRAPPLED

A creature that is Grappled has a speed of 0. If they are grappled by another creature, they may spend an action to roll Strength vs Strength against the grappling creature. On a win, they are no longer Grappled. On a loss, they remain Grappled.

BLINDED

A creature that is Blinded cannot see. It automatically loses Engagement and fails/loses any Skill Checks that rely on sight.

PHASED OUT

A creature that is Phased Out is invisible and intangible. While phased out:

  • It cannot be targeted by attacks or spells, and cannot interact with the physical world.

  • It perceives its surroundings in grayscale.

  • Other phased-out creatures can see and interact with it normally.

Entering or leaving the Phased-Out state immediately ends all Concentration (see Abilities).

CHARMED

A charmed creature considers the person who charmed them to be a trustworthy friend and acts accordingly. Rolls made by the charmer to influence the charmed creature are favored.
